analysis.one_liner: Lets victims of maritime and offshore disasters sue for full damages instead of a ship's value cap.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never received a hearing, vote, or floor action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: A 19th-century law lets a ship's owner cap its liability at the value of the vessel plus any cargo or fares owed. This bill would carve personal injury, wrongful death, and oil-spill-related claims out of that cap, so victims of maritime disasters could recover full damages. It would also let families recover for loss of companionship under the Death on the High Seas Act and the Jones Act, allow punitive damages in maritime cases, and apply the same death-benefit rules to general aviation crashes. It takes effect for claims arising after April 19, 2010, and for pending cases not yet finally decided.
analysis.who_benefits: Seamen and offshore workers injured on the job and the families of those killed; passengers and crews of ferries and cruise ships; victims of oil discharges and of general aviation crashes, who would gain the right to seek compensation beyond the ship's scrap value, including for pain, suffering, and loss of companionship.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Maritime workers and disaster victims' families

how_it_helps.text: Removes personal injury, wrongful death, and oil-drilling or oil-discharge claims from the rule that limits a vessel owner's liability to the vessel's value plus pending freight.
Allows punitive damages in maritime tort cases without regard to the amount of compensatory damages awarded.

Amends the Death on the High Seas Act to allow recovery for nonpecuniary loss — loss of care, comfort, and companionship — plus compensation for the decedent's pain and suffering, where current law limits recovery to pecuniary loss.

Amends the Jones Act so that, in claims tied to oil drilling or exploration or oil discharge, a deceased seaman's representative may recover for loss of care, comfort, and companionship, and lets the representative choose a jury trial at law.
Extends the aviation-accident death-benefit provisions to general aviation accidents, not just commercial flights.

analysis.who_pays: Vessel owners, offshore oil drilling operations, cruise and ferry operators, and general aviation owners, who would face uncapped damages, punitive awards, and higher insurance and litigation costs in injury and death cases.

drawbacks.text: The bill applies retroactively to causes of action arising after April 19, 2010, and to pending cases not yet finally adjudicated, changing the legal rules for accidents and lawsuits already underway.

Uncapped and punitive damages would raise liability exposure for vessel and general aviation operators, costs that could be passed on through higher fares and freight rates and that weigh most heavily on small operators.

The bill carves out fishing vessels: crews of charter and commercial fishing boats — among the most dangerous jobs at sea — would not get the expanded injury, death, and companionship protections unless the owner personally knew of the danger.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change targets a rule that could reduce a catastrophically injured worker's or a widow's recovery to the resale value of a wrecked vessel, and it was drafted in the wake of the Deepwater Horizon disaster, which killed 11 workers. The honest costs are real: retroactivity raises fair-notice objections, and uncapped liability would raise insurance costs for an entire industry. On balance, the bill's gains flow to the people hurt by maritime disasters, while its costs fall on the companies operating the vessels and rigs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

narrative.text: Senator John D. Rockefeller IV introduced the bill on August 5, 2010, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day.
One Senate Democrat cosponsored the bill; no other senators signed on.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action of any kind after the referral.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2011, and the bill died in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Vessel owners, offshore drilling operators, and cruise and general aviation operators came out ahead: they kept the liability cap and the limits on nonpecuniary and punitive damages that the bill would have removed.

for.name: Sen. John D. Rockefeller IV
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Commerce Committee, where he served as chairman; it was never taken up.

for.name: 1 of 58 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other senator joined.

sides.party_line_note: No recorded opposition: no committee or floor vote was ever held, so no one is on record against it; the bill simply never advanced, and its only two Senate supporters were both Democrats.

industries.industry: Vessel owners and operators (shipping, ferry, cruise)
industries.note: The bill removes personal injury, wrongful death, and oil-discharge claims from the 1851 cap that limits their liability to a vessel's value plus pending freight, exposing them to full-damage verdicts. Their interest in keeping the cap runs directly against injured workers' and victims' families' recoveries.

Claims relating to oil drilling, exploration, or discharge would be exempt from the liability cap, so companies could not limit payouts for disasters like a well blowout or rig explosion to the value of the vessel. The bill's effective date of April 19, 2010, reached back to cover claims from the Deepwater Horizon era.
Passenger vessels would face uncapped wrongful death and injury claims and maritime punitive damages, raising their exposure for onboard accidents.

The Death on the High Seas Act provisions would extend from commercial flights to general aviation, letting families of private-plane crash victims seek damages for loss of companionship and pain and suffering.

The bill explicitly exempts charter and commercial fishing vessels from its expanded liability and death-benefit provisions, leaving fishing crews — who work one of the most dangerous jobs at sea — with weaker protections than other maritime workers.
